missions.name: Riverwalk Weekend Mobility Surge
missions.description: Tampa's Riverwalk is absorbing more event traffic, ride-share pickups, and resident complaints than the curb network can handle on peak weekends.
learningObjectives: Compare visitor-flow interventions using operational evidence and stakeholder trade-offs.
Defend a curb-management strategy that balances destination access, resident quality of life, and visitor satisfaction.

stakeholders.label: Visitors
stakeholders.perspective: Want shorter waits, easier pickup zones, and a waterfront experience that feels welcoming.

stakeholders.label: Residents
stakeholders.perspective: Need sidewalks and crossings to stay usable during peak tourism periods.

stakeholders.label: Tourism operators
stakeholders.perspective: Need reliable access for tours, restaurants, and event guests without losing revenue.

stakeholders.label: City mobility team
stakeholders.perspective: Must reduce curb conflict, emissions, and emergency response delays.

constraints: The city can fund only one near-term intervention package before summer events begin.
Resident complaints are already in the mayor's weekly briefing.
Any solution that slows emergency access will be rejected.

evidence.label: Pedestrian heatmap
evidence.detail: Two choke points now hold visitors 24% longer than the district target during sunset arrivals.

evidence.label: Curb violation log
evidence.detail: Ride-share dwell violations spike at the same blocks where restaurants report late table turns.

evidence.label: Resident complaints
evidence.detail: Residents mention blocked sidewalks and unsafe stroller access more than noise or litter.

missions.reflectionPrompt: If you replayed this Riverwalk case, what would you watch first: curb throughput, resident access, or visitor wait times?

rationaleRubric.stakeholderFocus: Name the stakeholder group you are prioritizing most in this decision.
rationaleRubric.evidenceUse: Cite one specific data point or community signal from the briefing.
rationaleRubric.tradeoffReasoning: Explain what the strategy improves and what pressure it may create elsewhere.

exploration.brief: You are advising Tampa's destination management team before a run of high-attendance weekends on the Riverwalk. The mayor wants visible improvement in visitor movement, but community groups are framing the issue as a resident access problem, not just an operations problem.
exploration.mediaLabel: Pedestrian heatmap and curb turnover snapshot
bullets: Pedestrian dwell time rose 24% near two choke points.
Ride-share dwell violations increased at sunset.
Resident complaints cite blocked sidewalks and unsafe crossings.
exploration.description: Pedestrian congestion and curb conflicts are slowing visitor circulation and frustrating nearby residents.

exploration.brief: You are advising on immediate crowd flow controls before peak season weekends.
exploration.mediaLabel: Pedestrian heatmap + curb turnover snapshot
bullets: Pedestrian dwell time rose 24% near two choke points.
Ride-share dwell violations increased at sunset.
Resident complaints cite blocked sidewalks.

visualEvidence.caption: Pedestrian chokepoints cluster around two curb segments during sunset arrivals.
visualEvidence.sourceLabel: Source: Tampa Mobility Ops Dashboard (Weekend Snapshot)

exploration.alt: Annotated map of Riverwalk curb and pedestrian chokepoints during weekend peaks.
exploration.caption: Pedestrian chokepoints cluster around two curb segments during sunset arrivals.

options.title: Timed curb windows plus pedestrian marshals
options.description: Create timed pickup windows, add temporary marshals, and hold premium curb access to fixed periods instead of open-ended use.
options.feedback: The district moves more smoothly, and resident complaints ease because the curb becomes more predictable.
options.learningNote: This option works because it uses operational evidence to reduce friction for both visitors and residents instead of only protecting high-spend access.
options.coachNote: Notice how a mobility intervention also changes community trust and visitor experience.

options.title: Expand valet staging for event nights
options.description: Reserve more curb space for valet and premium arrivals to keep high-value guests moving quickly.
options.feedback: Revenue pressure eases, but the public realm feels less accessible and curb conflict gets worse for everyone outside the premium lane.
options.learningNote: Revenue can rise while destination legitimacy falls. In tourism planning, visible exclusion often has delayed but real costs.
options.coachNote: This is a classic short-term gain that externalizes the burden onto residents and non-premium visitors.

options.title: Festival detours with volunteer wayfinding
options.description: Divert foot traffic through alternate paths and rely on volunteers and temporary signage during peak windows.
options.feedback: Congestion softens somewhat, but the temporary plan is uneven and still leaves residents feeling reactive rather than protected.
options.learningNote: This is defensible as a low-cost stabilizer, but it does not address the root curb-management issue strongly enough for peak-season pressure.
options.coachNote: This is a moderate response: useful for quick relief, but weaker if your goal is structural improvement.

exploration.title: A) Expand paid valet and event loading zones
exploration.description: Prioritize premium curb usage to reduce queueing for high-spend guests.
exploration.feedback: Spending climbs, but congestion and emissions rise in adjacent blocks.
exploration.learningNote: Economic gains come with sustainability risk; pair this with a balancing follow-up mission.

exploration.title: B) Balanced systems package
exploration.description: Fund a cross-agency package that prioritizes weakest indicators first.
exploration.feedback: Performance improves across the board, though headline growth is moderate.
exploration.learningNote: This balanced mobility package prioritizes cleaner circulation and visitor experience while holding revenue growth steady.

exploration.title: C) Launch concierge shortcut lanes
exploration.description: Offer paid fast-lanes through the busiest sections.
exploration.feedback: Some guests are happier, but equity concerns and crowding persist.
exploration.learningNote: Economic gains come with sustainability risk; pair this with a balancing follow-up mission.

missions.name: Ybor Nightlife Identity Balance
missions.tourismDomain: Nightlife governance and cultural heritage protection
missions.description: Nightlife growth is strengthening Ybor's visitor economy, but local artists and heritage advocates say the district is losing the identity that makes it worth visiting.
learningObjectives: Evaluate how nightlife policy changes affect destination identity and community trust.
Defend a tourism strategy that supports evening demand without hollowing out heritage value.

stakeholders.label: Artists and heritage venues
stakeholders.perspective: Need programming support, fair visibility, and protections against being displaced by pure nightlife demand.

stakeholders.label: Residents
stakeholders.perspective: Want an active district, but not one that ignores noise, displacement, or identity loss.

stakeholders.label: Nightlife operators
stakeholders.perspective: Need reliable demand and predictable permitting to stay profitable.

stakeholders.label: Destination marketers
stakeholders.perspective: Need Ybor to remain distinctive enough to justify tourism promotion.

constraints: City council wants a policy package before festival season permitting closes.
Heritage groups have enough public support to block a license-only expansion plan.
Operators warn that sudden restrictions could reduce short-term revenue.

evidence.label: Nightlife permit trend
evidence.detail: Night permits rose 21% year over year, but heritage venue bookings are flattening.

evidence.label: Heritage venue utilization
evidence.detail: Friday usage of heritage venues is now materially lower than comparable nightlife venues.

evidence.label: Resident and artist testimony
evidence.detail: Community testimony emphasizes district identity, not anti-tourism sentiment.

missions.reflectionPrompt: What is the risk of treating culture only as a tourism product instead of a community asset in Ybor?

rationaleRubric.stakeholderFocus: Identify which Ybor stakeholder you are protecting most directly.
rationaleRubric.evidenceUse: Anchor your choice in at least one permit, booking, or testimony signal.
rationaleRubric.tradeoffReasoning: State how your option affects both nightlife demand and heritage legitimacy.

exploration.brief: The city needs a tourism-facing nightlife policy that can survive public scrutiny. Your recommendation must recognize that Ybor's culture is not a backdrop for tourism growth; it is part of the destination's core value.
exploration.mediaLabel: Permit queue and heritage venue utilization
bullets: Night permits rose 21% year over year.
Heritage venues report lower Friday bookings.
Resident and artist groups are asking for identity protections, not shutdowns.
exploration.description: Entertainment growth is outpacing heritage programming, creating backlash from residents and artists.

exploration.brief: Officials need a policy that protects district identity while managing demand spikes.
exploration.mediaLabel: Permit queue + heritage venue utilization
bullets: Night permits rose 21% YoY.
Heritage venues report lower weekend bookings.
Resident association requested a noise mitigation plan.

visualEvidence.alt: Trend graphic comparing nightlife permit growth with heritage venue utilization in Ybor.
visualEvidence.caption: Nighttime permit growth is outpacing heritage venue utilization on Fridays.
visualEvidence.sourceLabel: Source: Ybor Cultural Affairs + Permit Office

exploration.alt: Trend graphic comparing nightlife permit growth with heritage venue utilization in Ybor.
exploration.caption: Nighttime permit growth is outpacing heritage venue utilization on Fridays.
exploration.source: Source: Ybor Cultural Affairs + Permit Office

options.title: Heritage night bundles plus mobility and noise controls
options.description: Co-fund heritage programming, set mobility controls, and attach noise-management expectations to peak-night permits.
options.feedback: Ybor becomes easier to promote as a culturally distinct district, and evening demand stays active without relying only on license growth.
options.learningNote: This option treats culture as core destination infrastructure, not as a decorative add-on after growth decisions are made.
options.coachNote: Strong tourism strategy can protect the asset that attracts demand in the first place.

options.title: Fast-track additional nightlife licenses
options.description: Approve more high-volume venues quickly to maximize visitor spend before the next festival cycle.
options.feedback: Demand rises in the short run, but the district's cultural legitimacy weakens and backlash becomes more likely.
options.learningNote: Tourism growth that erodes place identity can eventually undermine the very differentiation that attracts visitors.
options.coachNote: This is growth without stewardship. It works until identity loss becomes the story.

options.title: Premium nightlife corridor with optional heritage marketing
options.description: Concentrate nightlife demand in a premium corridor and add a separate promotional campaign for heritage sites.
options.feedback: The district feels easier to manage, but the solution still separates growth from stewardship rather than integrating them.
options.learningNote: Segmenting premium demand can reduce friction, but it does not automatically protect cultural ecosystems.
options.coachNote: This is a plausible compromise, but it still treats heritage as marketing support instead of policy design input.

exploration.title: A) Fast-track additional nightlife licenses
exploration.description: Approve more high-volume venues ahead of festival season.
exploration.feedback: Top-line growth improves, but trust in district stewardship falls.
exploration.learningNote: Economic gains come with sustainability risk; pair this with a balancing follow-up mission.

exploration.title: B) Fund heritage-night bundles + mobility controls
exploration.description: Co-fund heritage events and coordinated transit/noise controls.
exploration.feedback: Identity indicators recover while visitor friction drops.
exploration.learningNote: Use this when your weakest category needs quick support without a major downside.

exploration.title: C) Build paid VIP festival corridor
exploration.description: Concentrate demand in a paid premium corridor.
exploration.feedback: Service quality rises for some guests, but exclusion concerns rise.
exploration.learningNote: Economic gains come with sustainability risk; pair this with a balancing follow-up mission.

name: Port Tampa Cruise Dispersal Planning
tourismDomain: Cruise dispersal, arrival management, and resident protection
description: Overlapping cruise arrivals are overwhelming nearby streets and reducing the quality of the Tampa arrival experience for both visitors and local neighborhoods.
learningObjectives: Use arrival-management evidence to compare dispersal strategies in a port tourism context.
Explain how visitor throughput decisions affect neighborhoods, downtown access, and destination quality.

stakeholders.label: Cruise visitors
stakeholders.perspective: Want a smooth transition into the city with clear routing and limited idle time.

stakeholders.label: Nearby neighborhoods
stakeholders.perspective: Need protection from idling coaches, spillover congestion, and sudden route surges.

stakeholders.label: Transport operators
stakeholders.perspective: Need predictable release timing and curb assignments to keep service on schedule.

stakeholders.label: Downtown businesses
stakeholders.perspective: Want cruise visitors to disperse into the district instead of staying stuck in transfer queues.

constraints: Two ships overlap on 14 days next month.
Neighborhood groups have asked for visible idling reduction.
The port wants a plan that improves dispersal without slowing overall releases dramatically.

evidence.label: Arrival overlap forecast
evidence.detail: Two-ship overlap produces the worst neighborhood pressure and longest transfer idle times.

evidence.label: Coach idle-time report
evidence.detail: Coach idle time exceeds target by 19%, especially when dispatch happens all at once.

evidence.label: Downtown dispersal signal
evidence.detail: Businesses report better cruise conversion when visitors reach multiple arrival zones rather than one saturated transfer lane.

reflectionPrompt: What is the tourism cost of treating arrival throughput as the only measure of success at a cruise port?

rationaleRubric.stakeholderFocus: Choose the stakeholder whose experience or protection your plan most directly serves.
rationaleRubric.evidenceUse: Use one forecast, idle-time, or downtown conversion signal to justify the choice.
rationaleRubric.tradeoffReasoning: Explain what your dispersal plan improves and what complexity it adds.

exploration.brief: The port authority wants a visible improvement before the next cruise cycle. You need a plan that protects neighborhood conditions while still moving large arrival waves into Tampa's visitor economy.
exploration.mediaLabel: Cruise arrival forecast and corridor travel-time map
bullets: Two ships overlap on 14 days next month.
Coach idle time exceeds target by 19%.
Downtown businesses perform better when dispersal reaches multiple entry zones.
exploration.description: Disembarkation surges overwhelm local streets and reduce time-in-destination quality.

exploration.brief: You need a dispersal plan that protects nearby neighborhoods and downtown throughput.
exploration.mediaLabel: Cruise arrival forecast + corridor travel-time map
bullets: Two ships overlap on 14 days next month.
Coach idle times exceed target by 19%.
Neighborhood board requested quieter rerouting.

visualEvidence.alt: Cruise dispersal route diagram showing timed coach releases and neighborhood protection buffers.

exploration.alt: Cruise dispersal route diagram showing timed coach releases and neighborhood protection buffers.
exploration.caption: Overlapping disembarkation windows create localized curb and coach idling pressure.
exploration.source: Source: Port Tampa Mobility Coordination Unit

options.title: Timed release windows with multi-zone downtown drop-offs
options.description: Stage departures in timed waves, use neighborhood protection buffers, and distribute arrivals across multiple downtown drop zones.
options.feedback: The city absorbs arrivals more evenly, idling drops, and the cruise arrival feels more like a destination welcome than a logistics bottleneck.
options.learningNote: A strong dispersal plan does more than move people fast. It shapes first impressions, neighborhood trust, and visitor conversion into the destination.
options.coachNote: This option balances throughput with place-based stewardship and better arrival design.

options.title: Priority coach dispatch through a single rapid lane
options.description: Use one dominant dispatch lane to maximize release speed and reduce dwell on port property.
options.feedback: The port clears quickly, but congestion and idling shift into surrounding neighborhoods and downtown choke points.
options.learningNote: This strategy improves one operational metric by displacing the burden elsewhere in the destination system.
options.coachNote: Throughput alone is not the same as destination performance.

options.title: Premium pre-booked transfers with limited staggered releases
options.description: Offer premium reserved transfers first, then release the remaining passengers in smaller waves.
options.feedback: Some visitors enjoy a smoother arrival, but equity concerns grow and the broader neighborhood problem is only partly reduced.
options.learningNote: Segmenting the best arrival experience into a premium product can raise spend while weakening fairness and destination legitimacy.
options.coachNote: This option is defensible if revenue is under pressure, but it is weaker on social license and broad destination quality.

exploration.title: A) Prioritize rapid coach dispatch lanes
exploration.description: Allocate most curb space to outbound coaches.
exploration.feedback: Turnover improves, but street-level friction increases.
exploration.learningNote: Economic gains come with sustainability risk; pair this with a balancing follow-up mission.

exploration.title: B) Balanced systems package
exploration.description: Fund a cross-agency package that prioritizes weakest indicators first.
exploration.feedback: Performance improves across the board, though headline growth is moderate.
exploration.learningNote: This package reduces cruise-area congestion and improves arrivals flow, with moderate upside for local businesses.

exploration.title: C) Add premium direct-transfer product
exploration.description: Sell direct transfers with dedicated loading zones.
exploration.feedback: Premium users benefit, but local impacts remain uneven.
exploration.learningNote: Economic gains come with sustainability risk; pair this with a balancing follow-up mission.

media.name: Busch Dynamic Pricing Fatigue
media.tourismDomain: Pricing transparency, value perception, and inclusive visitor experience
media.description: Visitors accept dynamic pricing at Busch Gardens, but frustration rises when families cannot tell whether the destination still offers fair value.
learningObjectives: Evaluate pricing strategies using both revenue logic and visitor trust signals.
Recommend a pricing approach that protects long-term destination value perception.

stakeholders.label: Family visitors
stakeholders.perspective: Need transparent value and fewer surprise charges when planning a park day.

stakeholders.label: Park operators
stakeholders.perspective: Need pricing tools that preserve yield during high-demand periods.

stakeholders.label: Repeat visitors
stakeholders.perspective: Compare the current experience against past value and fairness expectations.

stakeholders.label: Destination brand team
stakeholders.perspective: Need pricing to support Tampa's reputation for a worthwhile family attraction experience.

constraints: Holiday demand is approaching and management does not want to remove dynamic pricing entirely.
Refund requests are increasing among family segments.
Any proposal has to preserve some premium pricing flexibility.

evidence.label: Refund trend
evidence.detail: Refund requests increased on peak days where pricing and bundled fees changed most sharply.

evidence.label: Value perception survey
evidence.detail: Family visitors report that the biggest frustration is not price alone, but lack of clear value explanation.

evidence.label: Bundle attachment rate
evidence.detail: Upgrade bundle attachment is falling, suggesting some guests no longer trust the add-on structure.

media.reflectionPrompt: How should tourism managers distinguish between yield optimization and value transparency when pricing for families?

rationaleRubric.stakeholderFocus: Choose the stakeholder whose trust or margin you are prioritizing most directly.
rationaleRubric.evidenceUse: Reference at least one survey, refund, or attachment-rate signal.
rationaleRubric.tradeoffReasoning: Explain how your option changes both short-term revenue and long-term trust.

exploration.brief: Management needs a pricing revision before holiday demand ramps up. Students should treat pricing as part of the visitor experience, not just a back-end revenue lever.
exploration.mediaLabel: Ticket mix dashboard and value perception survey
bullets: Refund requests increased on peak days.
Family segments say value is hard to interpret.
Upgrade attachment rates are slipping.
exploration.description: Visitors accept dynamic pricing, but complaints rise when perceived value is unclear.

exploration.brief: Management is asking for a pricing strategy revision before holiday demand ramps up.
exploration.mediaLabel: Ticket mix dashboard + value perception survey
bullets: Bundled upgrade attachment rate fell 9%.
Refund requests increased for peak days.
Family segments report weak transparency.
exploration.alt: Busch Dynamic Pricing Fatigue visual anchor for eco park district.
exploration.caption: Ticket mix dashboard + value perception survey.

options.title: Publish transparent pricing ladders and family value bundles
options.description: Keep dynamic pricing, but show clear price ladders, standardize add-on disclosure, and introduce value-focused family bundles with explanation copy.
options.feedback: Guests understand what they are paying for, and value trust improves even without eliminating dynamic pricing.
options.learningNote: Transparent pricing can support both revenue and reputation when visitors understand the value logic behind the offer.
options.coachNote: This is pricing as service design: the explanation layer matters as much as the price point.

options.title: Increase peak-day surge and simplify only premium options
options.description: Lean into higher peak pricing and narrow visible options so high-spend guests convert faster.
options.feedback: Yield rises quickly, but fairness and trust decline, especially among families comparing the trip against previous visits.
options.learningNote: A pricing strategy that feels opaque or extractive can damage repeat intent even when it performs well in the short run.
options.coachNote: This is a strong revenue move and a weak destination relationship move.

options.title: Freeze visible pricing but keep hidden add-on variability
options.description: Hold the headline ticket price steady while shifting more value recovery into optional extras and service bundles.
options.feedback: The headline price looks calmer, but guests still feel uncertainty when the full-day cost becomes visible later in the journey.
options.learningNote: Stabilizing the headline price is not enough if the total trip cost remains hard to understand.
options.coachNote: This is a partial fix that treats perception at the front end without fully repairing trust.

exploration.title: A) Push aggressive peak-day upsells
exploration.description: Maximize yield with tighter surge multipliers.
exploration.feedback: Revenue rises, but sentiment and fairness scores slide.
exploration.learningNote: Economic gains come with sustainability risk; pair this with a balancing follow-up mission.

exploration.title: B) Balanced systems package
exploration.description: Fund a cross-agency package that prioritizes weakest indicators first.
exploration.feedback: Performance improves across the board, though headline growth is moderate.
exploration.learningNote: This package eases pricing fatigue and preserves guest goodwill, favoring retention and fairness over immediate yield.

exploration.title: C) Offer premium-only “frictionless day” bundles
exploration.feedback: Conversion improves for high spenders, but broad affordability concerns persist.
exploration.learningNote: Economic gains come with inclusion risk; pair this with a balancing follow-up mission.
